newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.

text.p: HOWARD READY TO GO IT ALONE ON TAX REFORM
Prime Minister John Howard says the Coalition will continue to push its tax reform agenda even if the Opposition continues to oppose initiatives such as a goods and services tax.
After mixed reaction to the Federal Government's tax agenda, Mr Howard has re-iterated his strong personal committment to improving Australia's tax system.
While business and retail groups have welcomed the Government's agenda, unions and welfare groups have said it will only benefit the well-off.
But Mr Howard is confident his desire for a more efficient tax system will be shared by voters.
A Government taskforce will soon begin considering options for tax reform, including cuts to personal income tax, offset by the possible introduction of a GST.
Mr Howard has refused to be drawn on what percentage a GST may be imposed at but has promised there will not be any increase in the overall tax burden.
He expects the taskforce to report within months.
"The Australian public will know well before the next election where we stand and that we stand for fairer system that gives individuals more incentive," he said.
He has again appealed for bi-partisan support for what he describes as a "great adventure" but intends pressing ahead with the process regardless.
"If we have to go it alone then of course we will," he said.
It's an approach wholeheartedly endorsed by Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett.
"I think it is a once in a lifetime opportunity and we Australians, regardless of our politics, cannot afford to blow it.
Mr Kennett is playing down the prospect of another election being fought over a GST.
He said a GST is part of the tax debate, but said it is not the "be all and end all".
And the man who had the job of selling a GST to voters in the 1993 election, Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith, is more confident of success the second time round.
Mr Reith predicts any Labor scare campaign will be rejected by the electorate.
HIGH COURT RULES KAKADU URANIUM LEASES ARE VALID
The High Court has found a mining company's leases to mine uranium in the Kakadu National Park are not invalid, overturning a decision of the full bench of the Federal Court.
Newcrest Mining was seeking damages from the Commonwealth.
The Federal Court had ruled the leases invalid because the Northern Territory Government renewed them after the Coronation Hill area, where the site is, was included in Kakadu National Park.
But the High Court has ruled that each of the mining leases is still in force and that the Commomonwealth acquired the property on other than just terms, as set out under the Constitution.
The case has ramifications for both the future of mining in Kakadu and the right of the Commonwealth to compulsorily acquire land in the territores under different conditions to in the states.
The Commonwealth had argued the leases were invalid because only it had the power to renew them.
BORAL THREATENS STRIKERS AS CAMPAIGN EXPANDS
The Boral timber company has threatened to stop negotiations over an enterprise agreement if its employees do not cease industrial action.
About 150 workers from Tumbarumba, in the state's south, are going to Bathurst today to join picket lines at the central west mill.
The long running dispute follows claims Boral has failed to offer union members the same pay increases given to individual contractors.

Boral has offered staff a $38 increase but more than 500 workers from hardwood and softwood plants across NSW have held rolling stoppages over the last three weeks, dissatisfied with the company's offer.
Bathurst workers set up picket lines at the mill yesterday and employees from Boral's Tumbarumba mill are travelling to Bathurst this morning to join their central west colleagues.
Caroline Betts from Boral said the talks will be threatened if the industrial action continues.
"Frankly, we've now reached a point where the company won't be able to continue to negotiate the enterprise agreement if that industrial action continues," she said.

Meanwhile, the miners' union has labelled as "desperate" a claim by management at the Hunter Valley number one mine that the union has doubled the money it will pay striking workers during future disputes.
The claim was contained in a letter from mine manager Alan Davies.
Workers received the letter just hours after the Industrial Commission handed down a recommendation which led to the cancellation of another planned strike.
Union official Mick Kelly said the union could not possibly double its strike pay to members, and the company's claims have further tarnished its image with the workforce.
OH, WHAT A FEELING' FOR PACKER
Businessman James Packer has struck a lucrative deal with Toyota to set up three giant car supermarkets in Victoria.

Mr Packer has teamed with his rugby friend and Sydney car dealer, Nick Polites, to try to lift company sales in Melbourne. Mr Packer and Mr Polites have bought the former Reg Hunt car-yard in the Melbourne suburb of Elsterwick in a deal believed to be worth $24 million.
It will become the first of three "super dealerships", which Toyota hopes will help lift sales in Victoria.
A Toyota spokesman said the expertise of the Polites group and the Packer equity is necessary to ensure the success of the site.
There will be some rationalisation of Toyota operations, with the Melbourne-based Pitstop dealership moving to the Elsternwick site.
Mr Packer is expected to only be an equity partner and not a car salesman.
SPORTS BRIEFS
SWIMMING
Australia has finished second behind the United States on the medal table at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships after the final night of competition in Japan.

Overnight, Grant Hackett won the 1,500 metres freestyle, Sam Riley almost broke the world record in winning the women's 200 metres breastroke and Mathew Dunn captured gold in the 200 metres individual medley.
RUGBY LEAGUE
The Australian Rugby League and Super League will meet again in Sydney today for compromise talks.
Heading the agenda is Super League's financial package, the number of teams and the name of any combined competition.
Super League's Ian Frykberg said he is hoping a peace deal can be worked out today.
Meanwhile, Canberra Raiders lock Bradley Clyde is confident of being right to play in Sunday's game against Adelaide despite the flu.
This morning St Helens won the right to play Brisbane in the World Club Challenge quarter finals, defeating Paris 42-4.
